summary: Paraguay admits Mercosur and associate-member nationals on a national ID card for 90 days and waives visas for EU, British, US, Canadian, Australian and many other passports for up to 90 days; remaining nationalities apply for a consular visa, or are invited by a host in Paraguay who files for a visa de arribo in Asunción. There is no eVisa.

passportValidity.text: Carry a passport valid for at least 6 months on arrival. Mercosur and associate-member nationals may enter on a valid national identity card instead, but airlines flying you in from outside the bloc will usually still want a passport.

source.name: Dirección General de Migraciones — Paraguay
Dirección General de Migraciones — Paraguay

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers arriving from a country with risk of transmission — in practice this catches many arrivals from Brazil, Bolivia and Peru. Paraguay has its own risk areas east of the Paraguay river, so vaccination is recommended for visits to the interior and to Iguazú-area border towns.

source.name: Ministerio de Salud Pública y Bienestar Social — Paraguay

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement. Public hospitals are free for emergencies but basic; visitors normally use private clinics in Asunción, which must be paid for up front, so cover is worth having.

source.name: Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores — Paraguay

onwardTicket.text: Airlines and immigration officers may ask visa-free visitors for a return or onward ticket within the 90-day allowance, together with an address in Paraguay.

source.name: Dirección General de Migraciones — Paraguay

proofOfFunds.text: No published amount. Officers rarely ask tourists for evidence of funds, but visa applicants must show bank statements covering the trip.

source.name: Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores — Paraguay

currencyLimits.text: Cash or negotiable instruments worth USD 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared to customs on entry and exit. The checks are taken seriously on the Ciudad del Este and Encarnación land borders.

source.name: Dirección Nacional de Aduanas — Paraguay

notes: Ciudad del Este is a duty-free shopping hub, but Brazil and Argentina enforce strict personal allowances on the way back. Keep receipts and stay under their limits.
Fresh meat, dairy and plant material may not be brought in; agricultural controls at the land borders are active.

Land-border crossings to Argentina and Brazil are not always staffed by both countries' immigration on the same side — get your Paraguayan exit and neighbor's entry stamps, or you will have problems later.

payments.text: Cards work in Asunción, Ciudad del Este and Encarnación hotels, malls and restaurants, but small towns, buses and markets run on cash. ATMs dispense guaraníes and, at some banks, US dollars; US dollars are also accepted outright in the border shopping districts.

safety.text: Asunción and the tourist circuit are generally calm, with opportunistic theft the main risk. Take more care in Ciudad del Este and around the tri-border area, and take particular care in the departments bordering Brazil, including Concepción, San Pedro and Amambay, where an armed insurgent group and organized crime operate.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Paraguay travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to September is Paraguay's mild, drier winter — comfortable for Asunción, the Jesuit missions and the Chaco. December to February is fiercely hot and humid, often above 38°C.

idp.text: Paraguay is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

driving.text: Paraguay is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Paraguay yet.

tips.text: Paraguay abolished daylight saving in 2024 and now stays on UTC-3 all year — the same clock as Argentina, Uruguay and most of Brazil. Double-check older guidebooks and booking sites that still assume a seasonal change.

On the bridges to Foz do Iguaçu and Clorinda, buses often do not stop at immigration. Ask the driver, get out and have your passport stamped in and out yourself — a missing stamp turns into a fine or a refused entry later on.
Tereré — cold yerba mate — is the national ritual and the easiest way into a conversation. Take the guampa when offered, drink it all, and hand it back to the server rather than passing it on.

December to February regularly passes 38°C with high humidity, and power cuts during storms can take air conditioning with them. Plan sightseeing for early morning and book accommodation with a generator if you are traveling in the Chaco.
Both Spanish and Guaraní are official, and outside Asunción Guaraní is what people speak among themselves. English is rarely useful — a translation app and a few Spanish phrases go a long way.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Paraguay?
faq.answer: For most Western travelers, no. Citizens of the EU and EEA, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Israel and most of Latin America enter visa-free for up to 90 days as tourists. Mercosur and associate-member nationals can even use a national ID card. Other nationalities need a consular visa, or a visa de arribo that a host in Paraguay files for on their behalf.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Paraguay?
faq.answer: Not since 2019, when Paraguay dropped the reciprocity visa for United States, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand passports and admitted them visa-free for 90 days. Because the change was made by decree and reciprocity policies can be revisited, check the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or your nearest Paraguayan consulate shortly before you travel.

faq.question: Can I enter Paraguay with a national ID card instead of a passport?
faq.answer: Yes, if you are a national of Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador or Peru. Mercosur and associate-member citizens can cross with a valid national identity document and stay 90 days. Airlines flying in from outside the bloc may still ask for a passport, so carry one if you are connecting internationally.

faq.question: Is there a Paraguayan eVisa?
faq.answer: No. Paraguay issues no electronic visa: travellers who need a visa apply at a Paraguayan embassy or consulate. The one alternative is the visa de arribo, and the traveller does not apply for it — a person or company in Paraguay does, at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' Dirección de Pasaportes y Servicios Consulares in Asunción, with an invitation letter, their own identity and financial documents and the traveller's completed non-resident visa form. Processing takes up to 30 days once the file is complete.

faq.question: Can I stay longer than 90 days in Paraguay?
faq.answer: You can ask the Dirección General de Migraciones for a prórroga (extension) before your 90 days expire. Many visitors instead do a border run to Argentina or Brazil, but repeated same-day runs attract attention. For genuinely long stays, Paraguay offers a comparatively accessible temporary-residence route. Ask a Paraguayan consulate about it before you go.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Paraguay?
faq.answer: It is required only if you are arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, which in practice includes much of Brazil, Bolivia and Peru. Paraguay has risk areas of its own east of the Paraguay river, so vaccination is recommended if you are heading to the Iguazú border region or the interior.
